questions.title: What is the precise legal distinction between the 'right-to-control' theory rejected in *Ciminelli* and the 'fraudulent-inducement' theory upheld in this case?
questions.question_body: I am struggling to understand the line the Fifth Circuit draws here. In *Ciminelli*, the Supreme Court said you can't convict someone just for depriving a victim of valuable economic information needed to make decisions. Here, the defendants allegedly deprived followers of accurate info about stock positions, causing them to buy. The court says this is okay because it's 'fraudulent inducement' to part with money, not just a loss of information control. Since both theories involve lying to influence an economic decision, what specific factual allegation in the indictment saves this from being a forbidden 'right-to-control' case? Is it simply that the victims actually handed over cash, or is there a deeper doctrinal difference regarding what constitutes 'property'?

questions.title: How does *Kousisis* redefine 'intent to defraud' when the defendant provides fair market value in exchange for the victim's money?
questions.question_body: The defendants argued they didn't intend to harm anyone because the followers received securities at market value (even if inflated by the pump). The court cites *Kousisis* to say that actual economic loss isn't required. I'm confused about the mental state element here. If I trick you into buying a house for $500k that is objectively worth $500k at that exact moment (but I lied about why I'm selling), have I really 'intended to defraud' you if my only goal was my own commission, not your financial ruin? How does the court reconcile the common law intuition that fraud requires a victim's loss with this new rule that obtaining money via lies is enough, regardless of the exchange's fairness?

questions.title: Why did the District Court dismiss the indictment initially, and what standard of review allowed the Fifth Circuit to easily reverse?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions the District Court dismissed because the indictment failed to allege a deprivation of a 'traditional property interest.' Since we review indictments *de novo* and accept all allegations as true, wasn't it obvious to the lower court that 'information' isn't property? I'm trying to understand the procedural posture: Did the District Court interpret recent Supreme Court cases (*Ciminelli*) too broadly by assuming any scheme involving social media misinformation automatically falls under the banned 'right-to-control' theory? What specific language in the superseding indictment did the District Court seemingly ignore that made reversal so straightforward for the appellate panel?

questions.title: Does this ruling imply that any 'pump and dump' scheme automatically satisfies the 'scheme to defraud' element under 18 U.S.C. § 1348 post-*Ciminelli*?
questions.question_body: The court seems to treat this as a classic fraudulent inducement case where investors were tricked into handing over money. However, in many pump-and-dump scenarios, early buyers might actually profit before the 'dump' occurs. If a follower bought during the 'pump,' saw their portfolio value rise temporarily, and sold before the crash, they suffered no loss and arguably got exactly what they wanted (a quick gain). Under this opinion's logic focusing on the *act* of inducement rather than net pecuniary loss, does every participant who bought based on a lie become a 'victim' for statutory purposes, even if they made money? Where is the limit on liability here?

questions.title: How does 18 U.S.C. § 1348 incorporate mail/wire fraud concepts after *Ciminelli* and *Kousisis*, and does it create different standards for securities vs. general fraud?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that § 1348 borrows key concepts from mail and wire fraud statutes. Given that *Ciminelli* and *Kousisis* were technically wire/mail fraud cases (or interpreted general fraud statutes), does this mean securities fraud now has identical elements regarding property interests and intent? Or does the unique nature of securities markets (where information asymmetry is inherent) suggest that courts might eventually distinguish how these precedents apply specifically under § 1348 compared to § 1341/1343? The court says there is 'scant caselaw' in the 5th Circuit on § 1348 specifically—is this gap significant?

questions.title: What role does the concept of 'material misrepresentation' play in distinguishing criminal fraud from mere puffery in social media trading contexts?
questions.question_body: The indictment relies on 'false and misleading information about trading positions.' In previous eras, influencers often used vague hype ('This stock is going to moon!') which might be considered non-actionable puffery. This opinion hinges on the idea that specific lies about *positions* induce people to part with money. At what point does a social media post cross from aggressive marketing or opinion into a 'material misrepresentation' sufficient for criminal liability under this new framework? Does the court's reliance on *Kousisis* lower bar for what counts as 'material' since actual harm isn't required?
